To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
spatial patterns in thunderstorm rain fields can be characterized using rain cells retrieved from weather radar and that this information can be exploited to improve hydrological modeling.

(a) spatial patterns in thunderstorm precipitation are highly variable, (b) these patterns can be quantitatively characterized using a rain cell approach, (c) these rain cell patterns can be used as input into a watershed hydrological response model and (d) the hydrological response to the spatial patterns can be quantified.

(1) radar-derived rain cells can be used in a hydrological model, (2) the hydrological response is strongly influenced by a single cell, and (3) a small change in cell location can lead to a large change in hydrological response.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach for hydrological modeling of thunderstorm events.
the development of an approach for the use of spatial radar data for the analysis of extreme rainfall-runoff events in a watershed.
the use of spatial rainfall patterns in the context of watershed hydrology and the potential of radar data for hydrological applications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
rain cells can be used as input for hydrological models, and that the spatial characteristics of rain fields can be a significant source of information for runoff prediction.
the spatial distribution of rainfall is an important parameter in hydrological modeling.
the hydrological response of this watershed is sensitive to the spatial pattern of rain cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the spatial patterns of rainfall are critical in runoff generation processes and that radar data can be effectively exploited in this regard.
radar data can be used in a watershed hydrologic model to simulate runoff response and to identify critical storm characteristics that affect hydrologic response.

radar-derived rain cells can be used to provide a detailed description of rainfall spatial characteristics that can be used to enhance the representation of rainfall in hydrological models and improve runoff response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spatial characteristics of thunderstorm rainfall events can be exploited in hydrological models to improve runoff predictions.
the proposed method can be used as a tool for hydrological modelers and water managers to assess and predict the impact of spatial rainfall variability on runoff response.

spatial rainfall information can be exploited to improve the representation of rainfall in watershed hydrological models and, in the case of extreme rainfall events, to provide a better understanding of the spatial and temporal characteristics of the rainfall and the associated hydrological processes.
